quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on how a woven construction is written and what each part of the weight calculation means.

questions.q: In the construction 20 × 20 / 60 × 60, 63", 1/1, what does the second pair of numbers (60 × 60) give?
options: Ends per inch and picks per inch
Width and length of the piece
questions.explain: A construction is written warp count × weft count / ends per inch × picks per inch, width, weave. The first pair (20 × 20) is the counts; the second pair (60 × 60) is the sett, EPI × PPI.

questions.q: Why is the warp yarn in one yard of fabric longer than one yard?
options: Because the yarn shrinks in sizing
Because the warp is wound under tension on the beam
Because each end bends over and under the picks (crimp)
Because the reed spreads the ends apart
questions.explain: Warp contraction (about 10 %) comes from crimp: the end weaves over and under the picks, so more yarn is used than the straight length of cloth. Tension on the beam and the reed do not add length.

questions.q: In the lecture, weft contraction is taken as about 5 % and warp contraction as about 10 %.
questions.explain: The lecture uses roughly 10 % for warp contraction and 5 % for weft contraction; the pick is longer than the fabric width by about 5 %.

questions.q: What does GSM stand for in fabric trading?
questions.explain: GSM is grams per square metre, the metric weight per unit area; oz/yd² is the corresponding imperial measure.

questions.q: Which of these is a weight per unit area rather than a weight per unit length?
questions.explain: oz/yd² and GSM are per unit area, so they do not depend on the width. lb/yd, kg/m and oz per linear yard all describe one yard or metre of the full width of cloth and change when the width changes.

questions.q: Total ends in the warp of a fabric are found from which two numbers?
options: Ends per inch and width in inches
Ends per inch and picks per inch
questions.explain: Total ends = EPI × width in inches: 60 EPI × 63" = 3,780 ends. Count and contraction affect the weight of those ends, not how many there are.

questions.q: Because Ne is an indirect count, a higher Ne number means a heavier yarn per yard.
questions.explain: Ne is indirect: one yard of one end weighs 1 ÷ (840 × Ne) lb, so a higher Ne means a finer, lighter yarn. Ne 40 weighs half as much per yard as Ne 20.

questions.q: The lecture calls fabric A (about 150 GSM, plain weave) a typical sheeting and fabric B (about 255 GSM, 3/1 twill) a
questions.explain: Fabric B, 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 in a 3/1 twill at 7.53 oz/yd², is described as a drill. Voile and lawn are much lighter cloths.

questions.q: Which quick check does the lecture give for converting ounces per square yard to GSM?
questions.explain: 1 oz = 28.35 g and 1 yd² = 0.836 m², so 1 oz/yd² = 28.35 ÷ 0.836 ≈ 33.9 GSM. The 25 belongs to the rough shop-floor rule, not to this conversion.

questions.q: Why does the lecture prefer the exact method over the rough shop-floor estimate for quotations?
options: The rough rule only works for twill weaves
The rough rule ignores contraction and width
The rough rule gives an answer in ounces, not grams
The rough rule needs the weave to be known
questions.explain: GSM ≈ (EPI ÷ Ne warp + PPI ÷ Ne weft) × 25 ignores contraction and width, so it is only an estimate. It works on any weave and needs no weave information at all.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Which formula, which unit, and which way the answer moves when a construction changes.

questions.q: One yard of a single end of Ne count yarn weighs, in pounds:
questions.explain: In the Ne system 840 × Ne yards weigh 1 lb, so one yard weighs 1 ÷ (840 × Ne) lb. 840 ÷ Ne would be the yards in one lb divided wrongly; 840 × Ne is a length, not a weight.

questions.q: Warp weight per yard of fabric equals:
questions.explain: Each end supplies (1 + contraction) yards of yarn per yard of fabric, and each yard weighs 1 ÷ (840 × Ne) lb, so multiply by the total ends and the contraction factor and divide by 840 × Ne. Dividing by the contraction would make the warp lighter than the cloth, which is impossible.

questions.q: How many picks are there in one yard of fabric woven at P picks per inch?
questions.explain: One yard is 36 inches, so a yard of cloth contains P × 36 picks; at 60 PPI that is 2,160 picks.

questions.q: The length of one pick is taken as:
questions.explain: The pick spans the full width (in yards, so that the Ne relation works) and is longer than that width by the weft contraction, about 5 %. Warp contraction belongs to the ends, not the picks.

questions.q: To go from ounces per linear yard to ounces per square yard you must:
options: Multiply by the width in yards
Divide by the width in yards
questions.explain: A linear yard of 63" cloth is 1.75 yd² of fabric, so oz per linear yard ÷ 1.75 gives oz/yd². The ×16 step converts lb to oz, which comes before this.

questions.q: If the warp count changes from Ne 20 to Ne 40 with everything else unchanged, the warp weight per yard of fabric halves.
questions.explain: Warp weight is proportional to 1 ÷ Ne; doubling the count halves the weight of each end and therefore of the whole warp.

questions.q: If picks per inch rise from 60 to 72 with the same weft count and width, the weft weight per yard of fabric:
questions.explain: Weft weight is proportional to the number of picks: 72 ÷ 60 = 1.2, a 20 % rise. Twelve more picks is a 20 % increase of 60, not 12 %.

questions.q: In the metric chain, lb per linear yard is multiplied by 1.0936 to give:
questions.explain: A metre is 1.0936 yards, so lb/yd × 1.0936 = lb/m. Dividing by 2.2046 then gives kg/m; dividing by the width in metres and multiplying by 1,000 gives GSM.

questions.q: For the same construction, a wider fabric has a higher GSM because it contains more ends.
questions.explain: GSM is per square metre. A wider cloth has more ends and weighs more per linear metre, but that weight is spread over a larger area, so GSM is unchanged (apart from small contraction effects).

questions.q: The rough shop-floor rule for Ne cotton fabrics is GSM ≈ (EPI ÷ Ne warp + PPI ÷ Ne weft) × k. What is k?
questions.explain: The multiplier is 25: for fabric A, (60 ÷ 20 + 60 ÷ 20) × 25 = 150 GSM. 33.9 converts oz/yd² to GSM and 16 converts lb to oz.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Work through the fabric-weight chain step by step, from total ends to GSM, using realistic constructions.

questions.q: A fabric has 60 ends per inch and is 63 inches wide. How many ends are in the warp?
questions.explain: Total ends = EPI × width = 60 × 63 = 3,780 ends.

questions.q: What is the weight of 1,000 yards of a single Ne 30 cotton end, in lb (to four decimal places)?
questions.explain: One yard weighs 1 ÷ (840 × 30) lb, so 1,000 yards weigh 1,000 ÷ 25,200 = 0.0397 lb.

questions.q: A warp has 4,000 ends of Ne 30 with 8 % warp contraction. Find the warp weight per linear yard of fabric in lb (to three decimals).
A fabric is 70 inches wide and the weft contraction is 5 %. How long is one pick in yards (to three decimals)?
questions.explain: Width in yards = 70 ÷ 36 = 1.944 yd; with 5 % contraction one pick is 1.944 × 1.05 = 2.042 yd.

questions.q: A fabric is woven at 60 picks per inch, 63 inches wide, with Ne 16 weft and 5 % weft contraction. Find the weft weight per linear yard of fabric in lb (to three decimals).
A yard of 63-inch-wide fabric contains 0.4838 lb of yarn. What is its weight in ounces per square yard (to two decimals)?
questions.explain: 0.4838 lb × 16 = 7.74 oz per linear yard; the yard is 63 ÷ 36 = 1.75 yd² in area, so 7.74 ÷ 1.75 = 4.42 oz/yd².

questions.q: A fabric weighs 7.53 oz/yd². Using the quick check in the lecture, what is its GSM (to the nearest whole number)?
A fabric weighs 0.4838 lb per linear yard and is 63 inches (1.6002 m) wide. Convert to GSM: lb/yd × 1.0936 ÷ 2.2046 ÷ width in m × 1,000 (to the nearest whole number).
Use the rough shop-floor rule to estimate the GSM of a 30 × 30 / 76 × 68 cotton fabric.
A yard of fabric contains 0.5280 lb of warp and 0.2953 lb of weft. The ounces per linear yard are closest to:
questions.explain: Total yarn = 0.8233 lb; × 16 = 13.17 oz per linear yard. 7.53 is the oz/yd² after dividing by the 1.75-yard width, and 8.23 is the lb figure wrongly multiplied by 10.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Merchandising and weaving-office situations where fabric weight decides the quotation, the yarn order or the complaint.

questions.q: A buyer asks for a 150 GSM plain sheeting. Which construction from the lecture meets it most closely?
questions.explain: Fabric A, 20 × 20 / 60 × 60, calculates to 149.96 GSM. The drill is about 255 GSM; the finer 30s and 40s constructions are much lighter (about 120 and 75 GSM by the rough rule).

questions.q: A merchandiser estimates a quotation with the rough rule and later the exact method gives a slightly different figure. Which is the most likely reason?
options: The exact method ignores the weft
The rough rule ignores contraction and width
The rough rule uses Tex instead of Ne
The exact method uses only the warp count
questions.explain: The rough rule leaves out contraction and width, so it drifts a little from the exact result (150 vs 149.96 for A, 254 vs 255 for B). Both methods use warp and weft, and both are in Ne.

questions.q: A grey-fabric contract is priced per kg. The mill proposes keeping the construction but reducing warp contraction by lowering the warp tension. What happens to the yarn needed per metre of fabric?
options: It rises, because less crimp needs more yarn
It falls slightly, because less yarn length is consumed per metre
It stays the same, because the count is unchanged
questions.explain: Warp weight per yard is proportional to (1 + warp contraction); a lower contraction means less yarn in each metre of cloth, so the fabric is slightly lighter and cheaper to make. In practice, though, contraction mostly follows the construction.

questions.q: A customer complains that delivered sheeting is 140 GSM instead of 150 GSM. The counts and EPI are correct. Which single change would most plausibly cause the loss?
options: Picks per inch woven at 52 instead of 60
questions.explain: Fewer picks reduce the weft weight directly: 52 ÷ 60 = 0.87, so the weft half of the weight falls by 13 % and the whole fabric by about 7 %. Larger contraction figures would make the cloth slightly heavier, not lighter, and an extra inch of width leaves the GSM unchanged.

questions.q: For a yarn-purchase plan, warp and weft weights per yard of fabric are needed separately, because the two yarns may have different counts and are bought separately.
questions.explain: The worksheet keeps warp and weft weights apart; fabric B needs 0.528 lb of Ne 20 warp and 0.295 lb of Ne 16 weft per yard, each ordered from the spinner in its own count.

questions.q: An export order is specified in oz/yd² but the local mill works in GSM. A 7.0 oz/yd² requirement is roughly:
questions.explain: 7.0 × 33.9 = 237 GSM. Multiplying by 25 (175) confuses the rough-rule constant with the unit conversion; 207 and 280 are wrong multipliers.

questions.q: Two mills quote the same 20 × 20 / 60 × 60 sheeting, one at 63" and one at 72" width. Which statement is correct?
options: The 72" cloth has a higher GSM
The 72" cloth weighs more per linear yard but has the same GSM
The 72" cloth has a lower GSM
The two cloths weigh the same per linear yard
questions.explain: GSM is per unit area and does not change with width; the wider cloth simply has more ends (72 × 60 = 4,320) and longer picks, so it weighs more per linear yard.

questions.q: A merchandiser wants to lift a 20 × 20 / 60 × 60 sheeting from 150 to about 175 GSM without changing the yarn counts. Using the rough rule, which change is closest?
options: Raise the EPI to 70 and the PPI to 70
Raise the PPI to 72, keep 60 EPI
Raise the EPI to 64, keep 60 PPI
questions.explain: By the rough rule, (70 ÷ 20 + 70 ÷ 20) × 25 = 175 GSM. Raising PPI alone to 72 gives (3 + 3.6) × 25 = 165, 64 EPI gives only 155, and lowering the PPI makes the cloth lighter.

questions.q: A costing clerk computes the weft weight using the width in inches instead of yards. The weft weight comes out:
questions.explain: The Ne relation (840 × Ne yards per lb) needs lengths in yards. Using inches makes the pick length 36 times longer than it should be, so the weft weight is 36 times too large.

questions.q: Which fabric would the lecture expect to be nearer 255 GSM: a 3/1 twill at 20 × 16 / 128 × 60 or a plain 20 × 20 / 60 × 60?
questions.explain: The twill has 128 ends per inch and coarser Ne 16 weft, so it carries far more yarn per square metre: 255 GSM against 150 for the plain sheeting.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the whole lecture: two-step reasoning, unit traps and the mistakes students most often make.

questions.q: A 40 × 40 / 100 × 80, 63" plain fabric has 10 % warp and 5 % weft contraction. Find the warp weight per linear yard of fabric in lb (to four decimals).
For the same 40 × 40 / 100 × 80, 63" fabric, find the weft weight per linear yard in lb (to four decimals).
questions.explain: Picks per yard = 2,880; pick length = 1.75 × 1.05 = 1.8375 yd; yarn = 5,292 yd; ÷ 33,600 = 0.1575 lb.

questions.q: The same 40 × 40 / 100 × 80, 63" fabric contains 0.2063 lb warp and 0.1575 lb weft per linear yard. What is its weight in oz/yd² (to two decimals)?
questions.explain: Total 0.3638 lb × 16 = 5.82 oz per linear yard; ÷ 1.75 yd² = 3.33 oz/yd², about 113 GSM.

questions.q: A student computes 4.42 oz/yd² × 25 and reports 110 GSM. What went wrong?
options: The factor should be 33.9, giving about 150 GSM
The factor should be 16, giving about 71 GSM
oz/yd² must first be divided by the width
questions.explain: 25 is the rough-rule constant for (EPI ÷ Ne + PPI ÷ Ne); the unit conversion from oz/yd² to GSM is × 33.9, so 4.42 oz/yd² ≈ 150 GSM.

questions.q: Fabric A and fabric B in the lecture have the same 60 PPI and 63" width, yet B's weft weight (0.2953 lb) is higher than A's (0.2363 lb). Why?
options: B has more picks per yard
B's weft is Ne 16, coarser than A's Ne 20
B is a twill, so its picks are longer
questions.explain: With the same picks per yard and pick length, the only difference is the count: 20 ÷ 16 = 1.25, and 0.2363 × 1.25 = 0.2953 lb. The weave does not change the pick length in this calculation.

questions.q: If both warp and weft counts are doubled (Ne 20 to Ne 40) with the sett unchanged, the fabric's GSM roughly halves.
questions.explain: Both warp and weft weights are proportional to 1 ÷ Ne, so doubling both counts halves the total yarn weight per square metre: about 150 GSM becomes about 75 GSM.

questions.q: Which combination gives the heaviest fabric per square metre, assuming equal contraction?
questions.explain: By the rough rule: 20 × 20 / 60 × 60 → 150; 20 × 16 / 60 × 60 → 169; 16 × 16 / 60 × 60 → 187.5; 30 × 30 / 80 × 80 → 133. Coarser yarn at the same sett is heavier than finer yarn at a higher sett here.

questions.q: A fabric weighs 0.8233 lb per linear yard. Express this in kg per linear metre (to four decimals).
questions.explain: 0.8233 lb/yd × 1.0936 = 0.9004 lb/m; ÷ 2.2046 = 0.4084 kg/m, matching fabric B in the worksheet.

questions.q: A mill forgets to include warp contraction when working out the warp weight of a 60 × 60 sheeting. Its warp weight is understated by about:
questions.explain: The true warp weight includes the factor (1 + 0.10); leaving it out gives 1 ÷ 1.1 = 0.909 of the real figure, so the warp is understated by about 10 % (9 % exactly).

questions.q: The rough rule gives 254 GSM for fabric B while the exact method gives 255 GSM. For which kind of fabric would you expect the rough rule to drift furthest from the exact result?
options: A fabric with unusually high crimp (contraction) in both directions
A fabric with equal warp and weft counts
questions.explain: The rough rule ignores contraction, so the more the yarns crimp, the more yarn the exact method counts that the rule leaves out. Balanced setts, equal counts and the 63" width are exactly the cases the rule was tuned on.
